title: A Powerful Truth: How Displays Of Strength Project Weakness
author: Jim Salvucci
summary: Jim Salvucci argues that conspicuous displays of power—from Soviet military parades to schoolyard bullying to a boss who never fetches their own coffee—are invariably signs of weakness, not strength. The central logic is borrowed from poker: bluffing is always a de facto admission of having a poor hand. Bullies, authoritarians, and insecure managers share the same tell: they need to project power precisely because they lack the inner security that makes power displays unnecessary. True leaders, by contrast, eschew ostentatious symbols and trappings of status because they have the 'intestinal fortitude to act with humility.' The piece distinguishes between boldness (which demands inner strength) and bluster (which requires only noise), and argues that the subtle, passive-aggressive power plays of everyday bosses—arriving late, cutting meetings short, redirecting perks for themselves—are just as damaging as overt displays. Real strength, Salvucci concludes, is expressed through choices that adhere to values and human decency, and true leaders need no external propping up.
points: Every display of power, large or small, signals deficiency: from Soviet military parades to the boss who strolls in late, each assertion of status is an implicit admission that the authority behind it is insecure.

Subtle power plays are as insidious as overt ones: the manager who redirects gift money to attend a faculty trip, or who makes you wait before starting a meeting, is making the same statement as a dictator crushing dissent—just more quietly.

The distinction between boldness and bluster is the distinction between character and performance: boldness requires genuine inner strength; bluster only requires noise and an audience willing to be intimidated.
True leaders actively avoid symbols of power even when those symbols are available to them, because they understand that expressions of power undermine morale and only weak people need them.
Leadership is expressed through one channel only: choices that adhere to values and a sense of human decency—not through entourages, puffed-up speeches, or demands for sycophancy.
quotes: A player with a poor hand will bet as though they have a sure thing, hoping to trick the other players into folding. The truth is that the player who attempts to bluff always does so from a position of deficiency. You wouldn't be bluffing if you placed a high bet on, say, a straight or a flush unless you somehow knew for a fact that your opponent held four of a kind. Therefore, bluffing is always a de facto admission of weakness even when the bluff works and the player wins.

Bullies never pick fights they don't think they can win. When they become adults, we call this 'punching down.' The whole point is to look tough, not to actually be tough—similar to a poker bluff. Bullying behavior exposes the true coward lurking beneath the aggression.

The bigger the parade, the frailer the leadership. During the Cold War, the Soviet Union was famous for its large military displays featuring a slow procession of tanks, missiles, and other armaments punctuating endless columns of synchronized soldiers. While an impressive sight and more than a little intimidating, the world knew that Soviet leaders relied on such spectacles to distract from their failures.

Bigwigs who bluster and boast are compensating for some shortcoming or other—real or imagined. No matter how successful the boss, you can bet that their tough-guy act is a cover for their lack of confidence.
Leaders don't have to show off because they have the intestinal fortitude to act with humility.

True leaders understand not to make choices that cut down, belittle, or oppress their team members. If—being human—they ever slip and fall for the trappings of power, they then will admit their error and correct accordingly.

Real strength derives from honesty and vulnerability, that genuine compassion and kindness emanate only from a solid inner core, and that maintaining decency remains the ultimate challenge. None of these qualities of character are for the faint of heart.
